FLUID: From Ephemeral IDs to Multimodal Semantic Codes for Industrial-Scale Livestreaming Recommendation

Xinhang Yuan Note: Core contributors. email: rose.yuan@tiktok.com Affiliation: TikTok, San Jose, California, USA , Zexi Huang Note: Corresponding author. email: zexi.huang@tiktok.com Affiliation: TikTok, San Jose, California, USA , Anjia Cao email: caoanjia@bytedance.com Affiliation: ByteDance, Shanghai, China , Xudong Lu email: luka.30@bytedance.com Affiliation: ByteDance, Shanghai, China , Zikai Wang email: wangzikai.kevin@bytedance.com Affiliation: ByteDance, San Jose, California, USA , Penghao Zhou email: zhoupenghao.leon@bytedance.com Affiliation: ByteDance, Shanghai, China , Chang Liu email: chang.liu.8@bytedance.com Affiliation: ByteDance, Singapore , Wentao Guo email: wentao.guo@bytedance.com Affiliation: ByteDance, San Jose, California, USA and Qinglei Wang email: wangqinglei@bytedance.com Affiliation: ByteDance, Singapore
2018
Abstract.

Modern recommender systems rely heavily on ID-based collaborative filtering: each item is represented by a unique ID embedding that accumulates collaborative signals from user interactions. Livestreaming recommendation, however, faces a unique challenge in this paradigm: a live room typically broadcasts for only tens of minutes, so its item ID remains poorly learned in a persistent cold-start state and ID-centric ranking models fail to generalize. We present FLUID, the first framework to fully retire the candidate-side item ID from a production-scale livestreaming ranker. FLUID couples a cross-domain multimodal encoder—jointly trained on short videos and livestreams to produce discrete hierarchical codes (LUCID)—with a late-fusion, ID-free design that injects slice- and room-level LUCID as independent tokens, stabilized by a staged warmup under online incremental training. Deployed on our industrial livestreaming recommenders with a cross-platform combined user base of over one billion globally, FLUID delivers significant online gains of +0.55%+0.55\% Quality Watch Duration, +2.05%+2.05\% Cold-Start Room Views, and +0.05%+0.05\% Active Hours.

Keywords: 
Livestreaming Recommendation, Multimodal Representation, Large Recommendation Models

1. Introduction

Livestreaming has emerged as one of the fastest-growing online content ecosystems (Zhang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2026), where creators broadcast in real time and users interact through viewing, commenting, and gifting. Unlike video (typical item lifetime measured in days to months) and e-commerce (months to years), livestreaming is dominated by one intrinsic property absent from those domains: items are extremely short-lived. On our leading livestreaming platforms with a combined user base of over one billion, a live room typically broadcasts for only tens of minutes (∼45{\sim}45 min on average), after which its item ID becomes obsolete. This poses a fundamental challenge for recommender systems, which rely on accumulating collaborative signals at the per-item level: as Figure 2 shows, the item ID embedding remains poorly learned within this typical 45-minute lifetime, leaving most live rooms in a persistent cold-start state. Modern large recommendation models (LRMs) (Zhai et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Gui et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026) place most of their capacity in ID-embedding tables. In livestreaming, these tables can only memorize short-lived exposure signal, which becomes useless once the room ends.

This short-lifetime vs. ID-memorization mismatch has motivated extensive research on injecting content-derived signals into industrial ranking systems. One line of work attaches frozen dense multimodal embeddings to items as auxiliary features (Sheng et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025). Another aligns or discretizes multimodal representations into compact semantic codes more compatible with ID-based ranking (Liu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Deng et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025), following the semantic-id line opened by TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023) and recent prefix-nn-gram parameterizations (Zheng et al., 2025). End-to-end multimodal recommenders (Liu et al., 2025b; Zhang and others, 2025; Yang et al., 2026) further train the multimodal encoder jointly with the downstream objective. Despite their diverse forms, a common pattern persists across essentially all of these systems: multimodal features serve as complementary signals alongside the dominant item ID in the ranking architecture. Even the closest livestream-targeting work, LARM (Liu et al., 2025b), whose encoder is trained purely on live data, does not depart from this pattern. These limitations point to two deeper, livestream-specific difficulties that remain unsolved.

First, producing a high-quality semantic ID for livestreaming is itself nontrivial. Live content is inherently multimodal and fast-changing (visuals, speech, on-screen text, streamer metadata, and audience signal all evolve within minutes (Liu et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2026)), and the ID must capture both transient dynamics and persistent room identity while tolerating the high noise of live signals. Prior work on multimodal encoders for recommendation is dominated by short-video or e-commerce supervision (Luo et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2024; Rajput et al., 2023), which is far denser and less noisy than live interactions; single-domain training on live data alone struggles to match that quality.

Second, even when a high-quality semantic ID is available, simply adding it alongside the item ID is insufficient. Multiple industrial studies have reported that, when multimodal features coexist with an ID-side signal, ranking models often default to the ID-side signal and underutilize the multimodal input, requiring explicit alignment, optimization rebalancing, or contrastive regularization to recover the multimodal contribution (Luo et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). This ID-dominance effect is tolerable when the item ID carries sufficient collaborative memory (as in e-commerce or short video). In livestreaming, where the item ID is ephemeral, the same effect wastes the main capacity of the LRM on a signal that quickly becomes obsolete.

To address these two difficulties, we propose FLUID (Framework for Live Universal ID-free Recommendation; Figure 1), the first framework to fully retire the candidate-side item ID from a production-scale livestreaming ranker.

FLUID’s two contributions mirror the two difficulties above. First, a cross-domain multimodal encoder jointly trained on short videos and livestreams transfers denser visual–textual supervision from the short-video domain to the sparser and noisier live domain, producing discrete multimodal codes we call LUCID (Live Universal Content IDentifier) as the sole candidate-side content identifier. Second, a late-fusion design injects slice- and room-level LUCID codes into the ranker as independent tokens, with a staged warmup that keeps the item-ID→\toLUCID transition stable in online incremental training and prevents the backbone from collapsing back onto the item ID.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    Problem framing: We argue that when the item ID is ephemeral, the widely documented ID-dominance effect becomes a fundamental bottleneck rather than a tolerable nuisance, motivating full retirement of the candidate-side item ID rather than further fusion tricks.

  • •

    Cross-domain multimodal encoder producing hierarchical LUCID codes as the sole candidate-side content identifier.

  • •

    Late-fusion ID-free ranker in which LUCID supplants the item ID, with a staged warmup that makes the transition safe under online incremental training.

Deployed on our industrial livestreaming recommenders with a combined user base of over 1bn, FLUID delivers significant online gains of +0.55%+0.55\% Quality Watch Duration, +2.05%+2.05\% Cold-Start Room Views, +2.87%+2.87\% Niche Room Views, +1.63%+1.63\% Unique Watched Tags, and +0.05%+0.05\% Active Hours.

2. Related Work

2.1. Multimodal Embedding

Multimodal embedding learning aligns heterogeneous data—such as images, text, and videos—into a unified semantic space (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021), enabling diverse downstream applications including industrial recommendation (Liu et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2025). Early work pioneered by CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) adopts a dual-tower paradigm with independent unimodal encoders aligned via contrastive learning, and has been extensively refined in specific aspects such as training objectives, architecture and applications (Li et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022; Zhai et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024a; Cao et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024; Tao et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2024). More recent work repurpose single-tower paradigms for deeper cross-modal fusion, leveraging the rich world knowledge and reasoning capacity of pre-trained (multimodal) large language models (Jiang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024c; Meng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025; Zhang and others, 2025; Liu et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2024). Our multimodal encoder follows this single-tower line.

Prior multimodal encoders for recommendation are also typically trained on data from a single domain, such as live streaming, short videos, or e-commerce (Liu et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2024; Rajput et al., 2023). In contrast, our multimodal encoder is trained on cross-domain data, enabling it to capture more robust and transferable semantic signals across diverse scenarios.

2.2. ID-based Recommendation Models

The dominant paradigm in modern recommender systems represents users and items as ID embeddings that carry collaborative signals. From early collaborative filtering (Sarwar et al., 2001) and matrix factorization (Funk, 2006; Koren et al., 2009) to Factorization Machines and their variants (Rendle, 2010; Juan et al., 2016), ID embeddings have served as the primary carrier of collaborative signal across heterogeneous sparse features.

Deep learning has further scaled this paradigm. Embedding-and-MLP architectures (Covington et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017) replaced hand-crafted cross features with learnable interactions; sequential models (Zhou et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019; Kang and McAuley, 2018; Sun et al., 2019) brought attention and recurrence to user-behavior sequences; and large recommendation models (LRMs) (Naumov et al., 2019; Zhai et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Gui et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026) pushed model capacity onto massive ID-embedding tables. The bulk of model capacity thus resides in ID-embedding tables, and performance degrades sharply when the ID signal is insufficient. This limitation is particularly acute in livestreaming, where item lifetimes are extremely short.

2.3. Multimodal Information in Ranking and Recommendation

While effective for long-lived items, the ID-centric paradigm degrades under cold-start or short-lived conditions, where insufficient interactions prevent meaningful ID embeddings from forming—an effect especially pronounced in livestreaming, where room identifiers are ephemeral by nature. To address this, recent work has explored compact content-derived semantic codes such as YouTube’s Semantic IDs (Singh et al., 2023) and TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023), and, more broadly, has argued that sufficiently powerful modality encoders can match or surpass pure ID-based models in cold-start regimes (Yuan et al., 2023). These developments point toward a broader trend of combining the memorization strength of IDs with the generalization capacity of content-derived representations.

Efforts to inject multimodal signals into industrial ranking systems can be broadly grouped into two families, distinguished by how tightly multimodal features are coupled with the ID embedding space: (i) dense multimodal features, where frozen or lightly-trained embeddings are attached to the item as auxiliary inputs; and (ii) alignment and discretization, where multimodal representations are explicitly aligned to, or compressed into, discrete codes more compatible with downstream ID-based interaction.

Dense multimodal features. A common industrial recipe attaches frozen multimodal embeddings to items as auxiliary dense inputs to downstream rankers (Sheng et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025). The approach is simple but suffers from two well-documented limitations (Luo et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024): representation mismatch with the user–item interaction signal, and representation unlearning, as frozen features cannot adapt to drifting preferences or business semantics.

Alignment and discretization. To close this gap, recent work either aligns multimodal embeddings to the interaction space (Liu et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025), or discretizes them into ID-like semantic codes via quantization (Luo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b; Zhang and others, 2025; Zheng et al., 2025); we adopt the prefix n-gram parameterization of Zheng et al. (Zheng et al., 2025) in our embedding lookup (Section 3.3). Despite their diversity, all these systems share a common pattern: the multimodal signal serves as a complementary feature alongside the dominant item ID in the ranker.

Our positioning. In contrast, FLUID fully retires the candidate-side item ID and lets LUCID serve as the sole content identifier on that side. We further train a dedicated multimodal encoder with cross-domain transfer from short videos to live streams, and target the extreme cold-start regime of live streaming (average room lifetime ∼\sim45 min). Table 1 places FLUID against representative industrial and academic multimodal recommendation systems along four design axes. Two of these axes are uniquely satisfied by FLUID: it is the only method that (a) retires the candidate-side item ID rather than letting the multimodal signal coexist with it, and (b) trains a multimodal encoder jointly across content domains (short videos and live streams). Combined with Late fusion and coverage of ephemeral items, FLUID occupies a design cell that no prior industrial system has jointly occupied.

3. Method

Figure 1 gives an overview of FLUID. The pipeline has four stages: (i) a cross-domain multimodal encoder (§3.1) maps each 2-minute slice to a 128-d embedding zz; (ii) RQ-KMeans (§3.2) discretizes zz into an LL-level codeword tuple—LUCID; (iii) a prefix n-gram embedding (§3.3) turns each LUCID tuple into a learnable embedding; (iv) a late-fusion ID-free ranker (§3.4) injects LUCID as independent candidate-side tokens, retires the item ID, and stabilizes the transition with a staged warmup.

3.1. Multimodal Encoder

As argued in Section 2, live rooms are too short-lived for the ranker to learn useful per-item ID embeddings, which motivates a content-side multimodal encoder.

3.1.1. Cross-domain Training Data

Livestreams on their own, however, are also too sparse on the query-to-item side: short broadcasts mean thin per-room user behavior signal. We therefore train a single multimodal encoder jointly on livestreams and short videos with a shared embedding space, where rich query-to-item pairs from short videos facilitates the training of the multimodal encoder and improves its generalizability.

3.1.2. Architecture

The multimodal encoder (Figure 1 top) consists of three components: a vision module, a text module, and a single-tower fusion module. The Vision Module, based on SigLIP2-base (native-resolution ViT) (Tschannen et al., 2025) with a two-layer MLP projector, produces visual tokens Tv∈ℝNv×DhT_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{v}\times D_{h}}. The Text Module tokenizes rich metadata—titles, OCR, ASR transcripts, author bios, audience comments, and sticker tags—into Tt∈ℝNt×DhT_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{t}\times D_{h}}. The Single-Tower Fusion Module, built on Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025), processes the concatenated sequence T=[Tv,Tt,[EOS]]T=[T_{v},T_{t},\texttt{[EOS]}]. Finally, the [EOS] hidden state is linearly projected to a 128-d embedding zz. We adopt a single-tower architecture so that vision and text interact across the LLM’s full depth, rather than only meeting at the output layer as in dual-tower designs. This single-tower advantage holds consistently across retrieval and classification benchmarks (Section 4.3.1).

3.1.3. Training Recipe

The encoder is trained on a query-to-item (Q2I) contrastive task with InfoNCE loss (Oord et al., 2018) and false-negative masking. Queries are user search terms or MLLM-synthesized keywords; items are 2-minute content slices drawn from both livestreams and short videos, with positive pairs constructed from user-behavior signals (likes, shares, and watch-through). To preserve the pre-trained semantics in the LLM, we train in two stages: (1) Alignment—only the MLP projector and output projection are trained; (2) Joint fine-tuning—the full model is unfrozen and fine-tuned end-to-end at a reduced learning rate. Within each batch, we discard entire negative pairs whose query embeddings have pairwise similarity above a predefined threshold to reduce spurious negatives.

3.2. Discrete Representation via RQ-KMeans

Using the multimodal embedding zz corresponding to the 2-min content slice directly as a ranker input is suboptimal: embeddings from a generic vision–language objective are misaligned with the user–item interaction signal, and a shared MLP over frozen multimodal embeddings lacks the expresiveness of embedding lookup tables of the ranker (Luo et al., 2025). We therefore discretize zz via Residual Quantization K-Means (RQ-KMeans) (Luo et al., 2025; , 2024) into an LL-level codeword tuple we call LUCID (Live Universal Content IDentifier), which would later enter the ranker through a learnable embedding table co-trained with other sparse-ID features. We use RQ-KMeans rather than RQ-VAE because RQ-VAE collapses codebook entries under our online streaming retraining cadence, whereas K-means gives stable partitions once fit. We set L=4L{=}4 and N=64N{=}64. The resulting LUCID is a tuple [c1,…,c4][c_{1},\dots,c_{4}], e.g., [33,42,63,3][33,42,63,3].

Slice-level LUCID captures 2-minute dynamics—a streamer briefly switching from chatting to singing—but the ranker also needs a stable room-level identity: user interactions accumulate at room granularity, and an identifier that changes every two minutes would force the embedding tables to chase a moving target rather than accumulate room-specific signal across slices. We obtain such an identifier by level-wise majority voting: at each quantization depth ll, pick the most frequent codeword across all cumulative slices. Because residual quantization already decouples coarse-to-fine semantics, per-level voting distills dominant content without mixing levels.

3.3. Prefix N-gram LUCID Embedding

Each LUCID code—whether slice-level or room-level—is a tuple [c1,…,cL][c_{1},\dots,c_{L}] with cl∈{0,1,…,N−1}c_{l}\in\{0,1,\dots,N{-}1\}. We now describe the way to map the tuple to a learnable embedding 𝐞LUCID\mathbf{e}_{\text{LUCID}} consumed by the ranker backbone.

Earlier approaches (Rajput et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2025) use level-wise decoding: Create LL independent embedding lookup tables 𝐄1,…,𝐄L\mathbf{E}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{E}_{L} with 𝐄l∈ℝN×d\mathbf{E}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}, and let 𝐞LUCID\mathbf{e}_{\text{LUCID}} as the concatenation of 𝐄l​(cl)\mathbf{E}_{l}(c_{l}). However, in residual quantization, deeper levels encode refinements relative to the prefix path: the same clc_{l} under different [c1,…,cl−1][c_{1},\dots,c_{l-1}] indexes entirely different semantic regions. For example, two slices with c1=0c_{1}{=}0 and c1=3c_{1}{=}3 that happen to share c2=2c_{2}{=}2 would both look up the same entry 𝐄2​(2)\mathbf{E}_{2}(2) under level-wise decoding embedding, even though residual geometry indicates that those two sub-regions are unrelated.

We therefore adopt a prefix n-gram embedding scheme (Zheng et al., 2025), which conditions each level’s embedding on the full prefix path—analogous to the classical n-gram neural language model (Bengio et al., 2003), but with the context made explicit as a composite key:

(1) c¯l=∑k=1lck⋅Nl−k,l=1,…,L,\bar{c}_{l}=\sum_{k=1}^{l}c_{k}\cdot N^{l-k},\quad l=1,\dots,L,

where c¯l\bar{c}_{l} uniquely identifies the path from the root to level ll in the quantization tree. With N=4N{=}4, the two collision cases above are now resolved: [c1=0,c2=2][c_{1}{=}0,\,c_{2}{=}2] gives c¯2=2\bar{c}_{2}=2 while [c1=3,c2=2][c_{1}{=}3,\,c_{2}{=}2] gives c¯2=14\bar{c}_{2}=14—different slots in 𝐄2\mathbf{E}_{2}. Each level-ll table is expanded from NN to at most NlN^{l} rows, and

(2) 𝐞LUCID=𝐄1​(c¯1)|𝐄2​(c¯2)​‖⋯‖​𝐄L​(c¯L).\mathbf{e}_{\text{LUCID}}=\mathbf{E}_{1}(\bar{c}_{1})\,\|\,\mathbf{E}_{2}(\bar{c}_{2})\,\|\,\cdots\,\|\,\mathbf{E}_{L}(\bar{c}_{L}).

The embedding at level ll is now a refinement of its own parent path, not a feature shared across unrelated sub-trees.

3.4. Late Fusion and Staged Warmup

The final step is to incorporate LUCID embeddings to the production ranker. Our ranker backbone is a transformer-like architecture (Zhang et al., 2026) based on token-level feature interaction, where different groups of feature embeddings are represented by different tokens. We now provide details on the incorporation of LUCID embeddings as separate feature tokens into our ranker.

3.4.1. Room-level and slice-level integration

Slice-level LUCID describes the current 2-minute content segment and captures short-term changes in the livestream, such as a streamer switching from chatting to singing. Room-level LUCID is obtained by the majority-voting procedure in Section 3.2 and provides a more stable descriptor of the live room. The two granularities are complementary to each other: the slice token provides transient multimodal evidence, while the room token provides persistent candidate identity.

Both embeddings use the prefix n-gram embedding scheme in Eq. 1, but they are parameterized by separate embedding tables. Sharing the same embedding tables leaves stable room semantics and fast-changing slice semantics into the same parameter space, which empirically weakens their expressiveness. We report the shared-table ablation in Section 4.3.2.

3.4.2. Fusion with the existing item ID feature

Let 𝐠\mathbf{g} denote the existing item ID embedding of the candidate item, and let 𝐬\mathbf{s} and 𝐫\mathbf{r} denote the prefix-n-gram embeddings of slice-level and room-level LUCID, respectively. The fusion strategies between content-based embeddings and ID-based embeddings can be broadly divided into two categories: early fusion and late fusion.

Early fusion first maps the item ID and LUCID embeddings into a single candidate representation 𝐡\mathbf{h}. For example:

(3) 𝐡replace\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\text{replace}} =𝐬,\displaystyle=\mathbf{s},
(4) 𝐡concat\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\text{concat}} =𝐖[𝐠∥𝐬],𝐖 a learnable projection,\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{g}\,\|\,\mathbf{s}],\quad\mathbf{W}\text{ a learnable projection},
(5) 𝐡gate\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\text{gate}} =α​𝐠+(1−α)​𝐬,α=σ⁡(f⁡(𝐮)).\displaystyle=\alpha\mathbf{g}+(1-\alpha)\mathbf{s},\quad\alpha=\sigma(f(\mathbf{u})).

where 𝐮\mathbf{u} can be the item ID embedding itself or side information such as exposure counters and item ID embedding norm. These formulations cover direct replacement, concatenation, rule-based gating, and learnable LARM-style gates (Liu et al., 2025b). And the backbone treats the final representation as a single token:

(6) 𝒯early={𝐡}.\mathcal{T}_{\text{early}}=\{\mathbf{h}\}.

Even though the early fusion strategy sounds intuitive in that it combines two item-side information directly into a single token, as we shall demonstrate later in our experiments, it fails to extract the useful information from LUCID due to the strong memorization effect of the ID embedding.

Late fusion instead leaves each signal as an independent token and lets the backbone learn their interactions:

(7) 𝒯late={𝐠,𝐬}.\mathcal{T}_{\text{late}}=\{\mathbf{g},\mathbf{s}\}.

This late fusion configuration allows us to fully leverage the strong interaction capacity of the ranker backbone to learn the incremental multimodal information from LUCID on top of the item ID.

However, keeping the candidate-side item ID after the introduction of LUCID limits the generalizability ceiling of the ranker model, especially for livestreaming ranking where item ID embeddings are often under-trained because rooms are short-lived. This limitation is empirically validated in our later analysis in Section 4.3.3. The final FLUID architecture therefore retires the candidate-side item ID completely and uses the room-level LUCID in its place, in additional to the slice-level LUCID.

(8) 𝒯FLUID={𝐫,𝐬},𝐠∉𝒯FLUID.\mathcal{T}_{\text{FLUID}}=\{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{s}\},\quad\mathbf{g}\notin\mathcal{T}_{\text{FLUID}}.

This design relieves the model reliance on short-lived item ID embeddings while preserving two distinct content signals to character the candidate item: stable room identity and transient slice dynamics.

3.4.3. Staged warmup in production

Directly switching from the item-ID-based representation to 𝒯FLUID\mathcal{T}_{\text{FLUID}} is unstable because the LUCID embedding tables are newly introduced and the downstream interaction layers have been trained around an item-ID-bearing candidate representation. The deeper reason this transition cannot be done in a single retrain is an optimization asymmetry between the item ID and LUCID. The ephemeral item ID embedding, although poorly generalizing, carries a strong item-level memorization signal that the backbone absorbs early in joint training, suppressing the slower but more generalizable LUCID signal; the resulting collapse is measured directly in Section 4.3.3. We therefore use a staged warmup procedure (Figure 3) that changes only one item-side component per stage, leaving the rest as a stable anchor.

  1. (1)

    Slice add-on. Initialize from a converged item-ID checkpoint and add slice LUCID as an independent token.

  2. (2)

    Item ID phase-out. Progressively zero out the candidate-side item ID, transitioning the model to rely on slice LUCID alone.

  3. (3)

    Room add-on. Initialize room-level LUCID tables from the warm slice-level LUCID embeddings tables and train them independently to specialize on persistent room identity.

After the third stage, we continue the production streaming online training schedule on the item-ID-free configuration with both slice-level and room-level LUCID.

4. Experiments

4.1. Experiment Setup

FLUID comprises two trained models that we evaluate separately: the multimodal encoder of Section 3.1, which produces LUCID codes, and the ranking model of Section 3.4, into which the LUCID codes are injected.

Ranking model. All ranking experiments are conducted on the production ranking dataset of our industrial live-streaming platforms, which collectively serve a combined user base of over 1bn. We adopt the full backbone, dataset, and training configuration of the production Zenith++ pipeline (Zhang et al., 2026) (dataset statistics in Table 2), and on top of the Zenith++ backbone we plug in slice- and room-level LUCID codes produced by RQ-KMeans with L=4L=4 residual levels and N=64N=64 clusters per level.

Multimodal encoder. The encoder is trained on a query-to-item contrastive objective jointly over short videos and live streams from our industrial platforms, following the recipe in Section 3.1. We evaluate it on an internal benchmark suite covering retrieval (live and video keyphrase retrieval, live taxonomy classification, video e-commerce retrieval, live I2I retrieval) and semantic classification, under both linear-probing and full fine-tuning settings.

4.2. Model Performance

Performance results. Table 3 compares four ranker configurations on the CTR target. Adding slice LUCID on top of the item ID gives a small lift, showing that multimodal semantics carry incremental signal. Retiring the item ID without a substitute (w/o item ID) is sharply negative, confirming the ranker’s reliance on item-ID memorization. Only the final configuration—retiring the item ID and replacing it with slice + room LUCID under late fusion and staged warmup (Section 3.4)—improves over the baseline on both metrics, showing that LUCID realizes its value as the item ID’s successor rather than a supplement.

Online A/B test. We A/B-test the three non-baseline configurations in Table 3 against the production ranker. Table 4 reports three groups of metrics—engagement quality, cold-start, niche content, and diversity, and retention—measured per live-card exposure for the first two and per user for retention. A Quality Watch is a deep (≥1\geq 1 min) or positive-action session (like, comment, follow, share, gift); Cold-Start and Niche Room Views proxy newly-broadcasting items and long-tail creators via low-view and low-comment rooms, respectively. Each arm reveals a distinct mechanism.

Baseline + Slice LUCID. Engagement and diversity move positive but retention does not. With the item ID still anchoring candidate identity, LUCID acts as a supplementary signal rather than a content identifier, so short-term gains do not compound into long-term user behavior.

Baseline w/o item ID (no LUCID substitute). Cold-start and long-tail metrics show apparent lifts, but every engagement and retention metric in this arm is significantly negative. Without the item ID, the ranker scores items less discriminatively and traffic is passively redistributed toward unfamiliar long-tail rooms; the resulting “diversity” is a by-product of degraded matching, not a genuine win.

Final design (baseline w/o item ID ++ Slice & Room LUCID). This is the only arm that improves every metric group simultaneously, and the only arm that turns retention net-positive. Because the diversity gains now coexist with engagement gains rather than trade against them, the broadening reflects deeply consumed content rather than reshuffled shallow exposure.

Together, the three arms isolate FLUID’s mechanism: multimodal signal alone cannot stand in for the item ID; retiring the item ID alone is a regression dressed as diversity; only by retiring the item ID in favor of LUCID does the ranker simultaneously restore matching quality, deliver genuine diversity, and convert both into retention.

4.3. Ablation Studies

We conduct ablation experiments to validate the key design decisions in FLUID. Ablations on the multimodal encoder are reported on retrieval and classification benchmarks (subsubsection 4.3.1); ablations on ranking components use CTR AUC unless otherwise stated, matching the ranking setup in subsection 4.2.

4.3.1. Multimodal Model

Our SigLip2 + Qwen3-Embedding single-tower encoder substantially outperforms an internal dual-tower CLIP-B/32 + Albert-V2 baseline across all retrieval and semantic classification benchmarks, with the largest gains on cross-modal retrieval. Table 5 ablates the three design choices behind this encoder—backbone (Qwen3-Embedding + SigLip2 over CLIP/Albert), fusion paradigm (single-tower over dual-tower with shallow fusion), and training schedule (two-stage alignment + joint fine-tuning over end-to-end)—and all three contribute consistent gains.

To more directly showcase the cross-domain effectiveness of our multimodal encoder, we inspect items assigned to specific LUCID codes. Because live streams and short videos share the same LUCID vocabulary through joint pretraining (subsection 3.1), items from both modalities can be visualized side-by-side under a common cluster. Figure 4 presents two representative clusters: (39,41)(39,41) groups swimming content and (17,26)(17,26) groups dance performances. Live slices and short videos remain semantically consistent under the same LUCID code, despite the substantial domain shift in visual and textual distributions between the two modalities.

4.3.2. LUCID Embedding Design

We ablate two embedding-side design choices that together shape how LUCID codes are looked up on the candidate side: (i) the embedding scheme, namely Prefix n-gram (subsection 3.3) vs. Level-wise decoding; and (ii) whether slice- and room-level LUCID codes share a single embedding table or use separate ones (subsubsection 3.4.1).

As summarized in Table 6, both prefix n-gram embedding (+0.11%+0.11\% AUC over level-wise decoding) and independent slice/room tables (+0.05%+0.05\% AUC over the shared variant) contribute positively, with prefix n-gram providing the larger gain. This confirms that resolving residual-level codeword ambiguity is the dominant factor in candidate-side LUCID embedding design, while disentangling slice and room parameter spaces yields a smaller but consistent additional gain.

4.3.3. Candidate-side LUCID Integration: Fusion and Training Recipe

Our deployment carries multimodal information only on the candidate side, which makes how slice LUCID is integrated with the existing item ID the key design question for whether LUCID can contribute incremental signal. This subsection ablates two dimensions: (i) the fusion mechanism, i.e., whether slice LUCID and the item ID are merged before the backbone (early fusion) or enter the backbone as independent tokens (late fusion); and (ii) the training recipe once late fusion is fixed, i.e., how to actually train LUCID and ultimately retire the item ID. Table 7 organizes all experiments along these two dimensions.

Fusion mechanism. As summarized in Table 7, none of the four early-fusion variants—parameter-free combinations (Replace, Concat) and learnable gates (LARM learnable, LARM feature) (Liu et al., 2025b)—improves meaningfully over the baseline (max +0.01%+0.01\%, min −0.13%-0.13\%). The LARM learnable gate converges to predominantly relying on the item ID (Figure 5), confirming that any pre-backbone fusion collapses onto item-ID-only behavior. Moving LUCID into an independent token (late fusion) architecturally breaks this collapse mode but, without a warmup recipe, still yields Δ\Delta AUC =+0.00%=+0.00\%, indicating that the bottleneck is the training recipe, not the fusion mechanism.

Training recipe. All variants in this block use late fusion. Naive training—from-scratch initialization (drop-nn) or with the EM3 CIC auxiliary loss (Deng et al., 2024) pulling LUCID toward the item ID token—cannot reach meaningfully positive AUC (best +0.01%+0.01\%), because pulling LUCID toward an under-trained item ID anchor only adds noise. Figure 5 further confirms that under the LARM learnable gate the model does not autonomously learn when to switch to LUCID. This directly motivates our staged warmup(§3.4), the only recipe that delivers positive AUC. Each stage carries distinct information: Stage 1 (slice add-on, +0.22%+0.22\%) confirms that slice LUCID carries incremental signal on top of the item ID; Stage 2 (item ID phase-out, +0.11%+0.11\%) reveals that slice LUCID alone cannot carry the persistent identity role; and Stage 3 (room add-on, +0.23%+0.23\%) shows that room LUCID precisely compensates for this loss, exceeding Stage 1 by 0.01%0.01\% and forming FLUID’s final design. Adding the item ID back on top of Stage 3 yields no further gain, confirming that LUCID has fully absorbed the candidate-side role formerly carried by the item ID. Slice describes transient dynamics; room takes over persistent identity; the two together fully retire the item ID.

5. Conclusion

In this work, we present FLUID, the first framework to fully retire the candidate-side item ID from a production-scale livestreaming ranker. FLUID couples a cross-domain multimodal encoder—jointly trained on short videos and livestreams to produce hierarchical discrete semantic codes (LUCID)—with a late-fusion, ID-free ranker that injects slice- and room-level LUCID as independent tokens, with a staged warmup that stabilizes the item-ID→\toLUCID transition under online incremental training. Deployed on our industrial livestreaming platforms with a combined user base of over 1bn, FLUID delivers statistically significant online gains across engagement quality, cold-start exposure, content diversity, and user retention. This points to a principle: when items are inherently short-lived, retiring the item ID is a more principled remedy than further fusion tricks for keeping the multimodal signal alive. We hope this work serves as a step toward content-grounded ranking in short-lived recommendation domains.
